hero.description: BS Psychology graduate from the Virtual University of Pakistan (CGPA 3.10/4.00). Undergraduate research on self-esteem and life satisfaction among diabetic patients (N = 200, analysed in SPSS), and supervised clinical psychology training in a district hospital setting.
hero.goal: Seeking master's study in clinical, health and mental-health psychology.

summary: I completed a four-year Bachelor of Science in Psychology at the Virtual University of Pakistan (session Spring 2022 – Fall 2025; degree conferred July 2026) with a CGPA of 3.10/4.00 across 133 credit hours. The programme was taught and examined in English.

My coursework progressed from introductory psychology to research methods, statistics (SPSS), psychological testing and clinical psychology. In my final year I took part in a quantitative correlational study of self-esteem and life satisfaction among 200 diabetic patients, which was approved by the Department of Psychology in November 2025.

Alongside my degree I completed supervised clinical psychology training at Isfandyar Bukhari District Hospital, Attock, and a community psychology project with women living in a shelter-home setting. These experiences shaped my interest in how psychological factors affect wellbeing and quality of life, particularly among people living with chronic illness or difficult circumstances.
about.researchDirection: I want to keep studying the psychological side of physical health: how self-perception, coping and social support relate to wellbeing in people living with chronic conditions, and how psychological assessment can inform patient-centred care.
goals: Pursue a master's degree in clinical, health or mental-health psychology.
Strengthen quantitative research skills beyond undergraduate level, including study design and statistical analysis.
Build supervised experience in psychological assessment and evidence-based practice.

research.title: Relationship Between Self-Esteem and Life Satisfaction Among Diabetic Patients
research.shortTitle: Self-Esteem and Life Satisfaction in Diabetes
research.institution: Department of Psychology, Virtual University of Pakistan
research.teamContext: Group research project completed by a team of four undergraduate students.
research.metaDescription: Undergraduate correlational study of self-esteem and life satisfaction among 200 diabetic patients (RSES, SWLS, SPSS): methods, results and findings.
research.summary: Undergraduate research project examining the relationship between self-esteem and life satisfaction among 200 diabetic patients, using the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale and the Satisfaction With Life Scale, with statistical analysis conducted in SPSS.
objectives: To find out the relationship between self-esteem and life satisfaction among diabetic patients.
To explore whether gender differences exist in self-esteem and life satisfaction among diabetic patients.
research.researchQuestion: Is self-esteem related to life satisfaction among people living with diabetes, and do men and women differ on either variable?

hypotheses.text: There is likely to be a positive relationship between self-esteem and life satisfaction among diabetic patients.
There is likely to be a gender difference in self-esteem among diabetic patients.
There is likely to be a gender difference in life satisfaction among diabetic patients.

background: Diabetes is a chronic metabolic condition that requires continuous self-management: blood glucose monitoring, medication adherence and dietary restriction. Beyond its physical effects, this ongoing demand can affect emotional wellbeing and how people evaluate their own lives.

Previous studies in Pakistan, Jordan, Poland, Iran and Turkey reported links between self-esteem, distress, stigma and quality of life in diabetic patients. The study's rationale noted that much prior work focused on the medical side of diabetes, and that gender differences in these psychological outcomes have been inconsistent across studies.

methodology.design: Correlational (cross-sectional) design, observing natural variation without manipulation.
methodology.sampling: Non-probability convenience sampling from accessible diabetic clinics and healthcare settings.
methodology.participants: 200 adults (100 men, 100 women) diagnosed with Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes, aged 30–65.
inclusionCriteria: Formal diagnosis of Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes for at least 12 months
Able to understand the purpose of the study and give informed consent
exclusionCriteria: Serious mental health conditions or cognitive impairment affecting participation
Life-threatening or severe acute medical conditions
Unable to read, understand or complete the questionnaires
methodology.dataCollection: After permission from clinic administrators, eligible patients received an explanation of the study and gave written informed consent. Participants completed a demographic form, the RSES and the SWLS in a quiet area of the clinic. Data collection was completed within one month.
ethics: Written informed consent from all participants
Voluntary participation with the right to withdraw at any time
Data stored and used solely for research purposes

instruments.name: Satisfaction With Life Scale
instruments.measures: Global cognitive judgement of life satisfaction (7-point scale)

instruments.name: Demographic information form
instruments.measures: Age, gender, education, marital status, type and duration of diabetes

findings: Self-esteem and life satisfaction showed a strong, statistically significant positive correlation (r = .674, p < .01): patients with higher self-esteem tended to report greater satisfaction with life.
Mean scores indicated moderate levels of both self-esteem (M = 29.25, SD = 5.65) and life satisfaction (M = 13.50, SD = 3.46) in the sample.
There were no significant gender differences in self-esteem (t = −0.58, p = .570) or life satisfaction (t = 0.58, p = .562).
Both scales showed good internal consistency in this sample (RSES α = .825; SWLS α = .788).
research.conclusion: The study concluded that self-esteem is closely associated with life satisfaction among people with diabetes, and that psychological wellbeing deserves attention alongside medical care. Because the design was correlational, the results describe an association, not a cause-and-effect relationship.
limitations: Cross-sectional, correlational design cannot establish cause and effect.
Convenience sampling from a limited number of clinics may limit generalisability.
Self-report questionnaires may be influenced by personal bias or mood.
Other relevant variables (e.g., socioeconomic status, family support) were not measured.
implications: Supports integrating psychological support and counselling into diabetes care programmes.
Suggests educational programmes and support groups that build patients' confidence in managing their condition.
Points to further research on psychological wellbeing and diabetes outcomes.
research.reflection: This project was my first experience of carrying a study from proposal to final report: reviewing literature, working with standardised instruments, collecting data with informed consent, and interpreting statistical output honestly, including the hypotheses that were not supported. It strengthened my interest in health psychology and in how psychological factors relate to living with chronic illness.

projects.title: Active Citizenship: Pathways to Healing
projects.description: Group community-based project with women living in a shelter-home setting. I contributed the literature review section on art therapy and psychological healing, and helped plan and facilitate art-based activities: My Inner World, Safe Places, Freedom and Hope, and My Identity.
projects.outcome: The project report recorded increased participant engagement, emotional expression and social interaction. These outcomes were based on qualitative observation and participant feedback, not standardised pre/post measurement.
projects.confidentialityNote: The project report contains photographs and artwork of participants from a vulnerable population, so it is not published online.
